headings.title: Introduction and Indications for Tracheotomy
headings.content: A tracheotomy is a surgical procedure that creates an opening into the trachea through the neck to establish a secure airway. As nursing students preparing for clinical practice, understanding the primary indications for this procedure is vital for rapid patient assessment and interprofessional care planning. Common clinical indications include acute or chronic upper airway obstruction caused by tumors, severe trauma, foreign bodies, or laryngeal edema. Additionally, prolonged mechanical ventilation is a frequent indication, as a tracheostomy reduces the work of breathing, minimizes laryngeal and vocal cord damage associated with prolonged endotracheal intubation, and allows for easier oral hygiene and patient comfort. Other indications encompass neuromuscular diseases that lead to respiratory muscle weakness and an inability to clear copious pulmonary secretions independently. In emergency settings, an urgent surgical or percutaneous tracheotomy may be performed when orotracheal intubation fails. Nurses must recognize the underlying etiology for the tracheostomy, as this directly influences the patient's respiratory baseline, care plan, prognosis, and potential for future decannulation. Continuous vigilance is required to identify clinical deterioration, monitor oxygen saturation, and ensure the airway remains patent and free from obstruction.

headings.title: Anatomy of the Trachea and Surgical Landmarks
headings.content: A thorough understanding of the anatomical structures of the trachea and surrounding neck landmarks is critical for safe nursing care and assisting during surgical airway placement. The trachea is a flexible, tubular airway extending from the larynx down to the mainstem bronchi, supported by C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage that prevent airway collapse during inspiration. For healthcare professionals caring for patients with a tracheostomy, identifying key surface landmarks is essential for safe dressing changes, tie replacements, and tube repositioning. These landmarks include the thyroid cartilage (commonly known as the Adam's apple), the cricoid cartilage, and the suprasternal notch. The surgical creation of a tracheostomy typically occurs between the second and third or third and fourth tracheal rings. Surrounding anatomical structures that demand vigilant nursing awareness include the thyroid gland, the carotid arteries, the jugular veins, and the recurrent laryngeal nerves. Accidental dislodgement or improper tube sizing can pose severe risks due to the proximity of these major vascular and neurological structures. Nurses must document the position of the tracheostomy faceplate relative to these landmarks and report any abnormal swelling, hematoma formation, or anatomical displacement immediately to the medical team.

headings.title: Types of Tracheostomy Tubes and Components
headings.content: Tracheostomy tubes vary in material, design, and presence of a cuff, each serving distinct clinical purposes for patient management. Tubes can be constructed from plastics like polyvinyl chloride (PVC), silicone, or metals such as silver. A standard tracheostomy tube assembly consists of an outer cannula (which remains in place to maintain the airway tract), an inner cannula (which can be removed, cleaned, or replaced to prevent mucus plugging), and an obturator (used solely during insertion to guide the tube smoothly and prevent trauma to the tracheal wall). Cuffed tubes are utilized for patients who require mechanical ventilation or are at high risk of aspiration, as the inflated cuff creates a seal against the tracheal wall. However, cuff pressure must be monitored regularly to prevent mucosal ischemia and necrosis. Uncuffed tubes are used for patients who are breathing independently, have a low risk of aspiration, and are in the process of weaning or speaking. Some tubes also feature a fenestration—a small opening on the outer shaft that allows air to pass upward through the vocal cords, enabling the patient to speak when a cap is placed and the cuff is deflated. Nurses must verify tube specifications, manufacturer guidelines, and compatibility before performing any routine maintenance or tube changes.

headings.title: Emergency Tracheostomy Care and Maintenance
headings.content: Emergency tracheostomy care and routine maintenance are core competencies for nursing students working in critical care, step-down, or general medical-surgical wards. Every patient with a tracheostomy must have an emergency bedside kit immediately accessible. This kit must contain a spare tracheostomy tube of the exact same size, a spare tube one size smaller, a matching obturator, a bag-valve-mask (BVM) resuscitator, sterile suction catheters, normal saline, and a functional suction machine. In the event of accidental decannulation or total tube obstruction, rapid action is lifesaving. If a tube is accidentally dislodged within the first few postoperative days, it represents a surgical emergency because the tract has not yet matured; the nurse must call for immediate medical assistance while attempting to secure the airway. For a mature tract, the nurse may gently insert the obturator-loaded spare tube into the stoma, remove the obturator, secure the ties, and assess breath sounds and chest rise. Routine maintenance involves cleaning the peristomal skin with sterile saline or mild antiseptic as prescribed, keeping the area dry to prevent skin breakdown, and changing tracheostomy ties using a secure two-person technique to prevent accidental dislodgement. Nurses must document all interventions, stoma appearance, and patient tolerance clearly.

headings.title: Routine Nursing Assessment and Monitoring
headings.content: Routine nursing assessment and monitoring of a patient with a tracheostomy require systematic evaluation of respiratory status, airway patency, and the surrounding stoma site. Nurses must perform comprehensive respiratory assessments at least every shift, or more frequently based on clinical acuity. This includes auscultating bilateral breath sounds to detect adventitious sounds such as rhonchi or wheezes, monitoring oxygen saturation via pulse oximetry, assessing respiratory rate, depth, and effort, and observing chest symmetry. The stoma site and peristomal skin must be inspected regularly for signs of infection (such as purulent drainage, foul odor, erythema, and warmth), skin breakdown, and subcutaneous emphysema. Cuff pressure should be monitored and maintained within the safe recommended range of 20 to 25 mmHg (or 25 to 30 cmH2O) using a specialized manometer to prevent tracheal mucosal ischemia, necrosis, or tracheal-esophageal fistula formation. Humidification is another vital aspect of care, as bypassing the upper airway prevents natural warming and humidification of inspired air, leading to thick, tenacious secretions. Nurses must ensure continuous delivery of warmed, humidified oxygen or room air via a tracheostomy collar or T-piece and encourage adequate systemic hydration unless contraindicated.

headings.title: Suctioning Techniques and Airway Clearance
headings.content: Suctioning is a crucial airway clearance technique performed to remove accumulated mucus, blood, or foreign material when the patient is unable to clear secretions effectively through coughing. Nursing students must master both open and closed (inline) suctioning techniques while adhering strictly to aseptic principles. Before initiating suctioning, the nurse should assess clinical indicators such as audible gurgling, visible secretions in the tube, coughing, increased peak inspiratory pressures on a ventilator, or a drop in oxygen saturation. Pre-oxygenation with 100% oxygen for 30 to 60 seconds is essential to prevent hypoxia during the procedure. The suction catheter diameter should not exceed half the internal diameter of the tracheostomy tube to prevent negative pressure trauma. During insertion, the suction control port must remain open; suction is applied only intermittently using a rotating motion during withdrawal, and the total duration of each suction pass must not exceed 10 to 15 seconds to minimize oxygen depletion and mucosal irritation. Saline instillation directly into the tracheostomy tube is no longer routinely recommended due to risks of driving bacteria deeper into the lungs and causing oxygen desaturation, unless specifically ordered for thick, tenacious mucus that fails to clear. Post-procedure assessment includes re-evaluating breath sounds, vital signs, and patient comfort.

headings.title: Complications and Crisis Management
headings.content: Managing complications associated with a tracheostomy requires rapid recognition, critical thinking, and decisive nursing intervention. Early complications include hemorrhage at the surgical site, pneumothorax, subcutaneous emphysema, and accidental decannulation. Late complications encompass tracheal stenosis, tracheomalacia, infection, tracheocutaneous fistula, and tracheo-arterial fistula (a catastrophic erosion of the posterior wall of the trachea into the innominate artery). Nurses must be particularly vigilant for sentinel bleeds or pulsatile movement of the tracheostomy tube, which can indicate an impending erosion of the innominate artery; this demands immediate manual compression and surgical notification. Obstruction of the tube by thick mucus plugs can lead to acute respiratory distress, severe hypoxemia, and cyanosis. If obstruction is suspected, the nurse should immediately attempt to suction the tube, remove and clean the inner cannula, or replace it if it is a disposable/nondisposable unit. If the airway remains blocked despite these measures, bag-valve-mask ventilation should be attempted, and the rapid response team or attending physician must be activated immediately. Maintaining calm, structured communication during a crisis ensures patient safety and optimizes clinical outcomes.

headings.title: Weaning, Decannulation, and Patient Education
headings.content: The final phases of tracheostomy care involve weaning, decannulation, and comprehensive patient and family education. Weaning begins when the patient's underlying respiratory condition improves, airway protection reflexes are intact, and they can tolerate spontaneous breathing without full ventilator support. Nurses assist in the weaning process by participating in trials of progressive cuff deflation, implementing speaking valves (such as a Passy-Muir valve) to restore phonation, and utilizing progressively smaller tracheostomy tubes or button caps (capping trials) to encourage upper airway breathing. Decannulation is the permanent removal of the tracheostomy tube once the patient successfully tolerates 24 to 48 hours of complete tube capping. Following decannulation, the stoma is covered with an occlusive sterile dressing secured firmly with tape to prevent air leakage and allow secondary intention healing. Patient and family education is paramount for safe transition to home care. Nurses must teach patients and caregivers how to perform effective suctioning, recognize signs of respiratory distress, clean the stoma site, change ties and inner cannulas, and access emergency services. Clear, empathetic teaching empowers patients to achieve independence and reduces hospital readmission rates.
